Supervisor Shu Li

notes: Good afternoon, professors. I am Xuliang Zhu. My dissertation covers the DarkSHINE simulation framework and a prospective search with a positron beam. I will begin with the physics motivation, explain our software work, and then discuss the positron analysis and its expected sensitivity.

title: Outline
body:
Outline

01Physics Motivation and
DarkSHINE Experiment
02Event Simulation and
Reconstruction in DarkSHINE

Analysis
04Summary and Outlook
notes: I will start with the physics motivation and detector requirements, then introduce the simulation and reconstruction framework. I will then present our study of 3 production mechanisms with a positron beam. My focus is on the experimental work: simulating rare backgrounds efficiently, selecting signal events, and estimating the sensitivity. I will explain the theory assumptions where we need them.

title: Physics Motivation and DarkSHINE Experiment
body:
01 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Physics Motivation and
DarkSHINE Experiment

Light dark matter and an accelerator-based missing-energy search
notes: Gravitational observations give us evidence for dark matter. To search for it in the laboratory, we need a model of how it interacts with ordinary matter.

title: Evidence for dark matter
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Evidence for dark matter

Extended mass distributions

Orbital velocities remain high beyond the luminous disc.

Mass and gas separate

Lensing traces gravitating matter beyond the hot gas.

A non-baryonic component

The matter budget is constrained across cosmic scales.

These observations constrain the abundance and distribution of dark matter; its particle identity remains unknown.
Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018.
notes: We see evidence for dark matter over a wide range of scales, from galaxy rotation curves to cluster lensing and the cosmic microwave background. In merging clusters, the hot gas and the mass inferred from lensing can be spatially separated. Together, these observations give us information about the abundance and distribution of dark matter. Its particle identity and its coupling to ordinary matter remain unknown.
source: Clowe et al., ApJ 648 (2006) L109; Planck 2018. Image: supplied reference assets.

title: What observations constrain
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# What observations constrain

Observational requirements

Long-lived on cosmological time scales.

Sufficiently cold to form the observed structures.

Model-dependent bounds

Statistics, thermal history and late energy injection determine the relevant limits.
notes: The observations constrain different properties of dark matter. Its lifetime has to be long enough for it to survive until today, and its motion in the early Universe has to be consistent with the small-scale structure we observe. The phase-space bound applies to fermions. Thermal free-streaming bounds depend on the assumed early velocity distribution. BBN (Big Bang Nucleosynthesis) and the CMB (Cosmic Microwave Background) constrain new species in thermal contact with the Standard Model, as well as later energy injection. These constraints motivate searches for light dark matter, but they rely on different assumptions and do not give a single lower mass limit for every model. For this study, we use a vector-portal benchmark in the MeV to GeV range.

title: Complementary dark-matter searches
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Complementary dark-matter searches
DarkSHINE probes controlled production through missing energy and momentum.
notes: Direct detection looks for interactions of Galactic dark matter in a detector. It becomes difficult when the recoil energy is very small. Indirect detection looks for products of dark-matter annihilation or decay. At an accelerator, we try to produce dark matter in a controlled collision. We know the beam energy, so we can search for events with less visible energy than expected. This search does not depend on the local halo density. Relating the result to the cosmic abundance still requires a dark-sector model. The experimental challenge is to reject ordinary interactions in which visible particles escape detection.

title: The dark photon as a vector portal
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# The dark photon as a vector portal
01Production

Kinetic mixing

After diagonalising the kinetic terms, the mediator couples to the electromagnetic current:

Production rates scale approximately as .

02Invisible decay

Invisible benchmark

Dark-sector coupling .

For , assume

Experimental coordinates: .

Invisible dark-photon production gives a missing-energy signature.
notes:
This equation describes kinetic mixing between the photon and the dark photon. The parameter epsilon gives the dark photon a small coupling to the electromagnetic current. Its mass determines the kinematics, and epsilon squared approximately scales the production rate. We assume that the dark photon can decay to lighter dark-sector particles, with an invisible branching fraction close to 1. I therefore show the projected limits as a function of mediator mass and kinetic mixing. Later, when comparing with thermal relic targets, I will specify the dark coupling and the mass ratio. We do not need to choose a detailed ultraviolet model for this detector study.

Presenter cue: Start with production through kinetic mixing. Click once to introduce invisible decay and the benchmark assumptions.

title: SHINE facility and DarkSHINE beamline
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# SHINE facility and DarkSHINE beamline
Beam benchmark

A high-repetition-rate source

Shanghai High Repetition-Rate XFEL and Extreme Light Facility

8 GeVReference beam energy
1 MHzNominal single-particle rate

Benchmark: incident particles.

A dedicated extraction branch provides the basis for the electron programme. Positron delivery is a prospective extension.
notes: SHINE (Shanghai High Repetition-Rate XFEL (X-ray Free-Electron Laser) and Extreme Light Facility) provides the accelerator for DarkSHINE. The electron programme uses a dedicated single-particle extraction branch alongside the FEL (Free-Electron Laser) beamlines. The reference beam energy is 8 GeV, and the benchmark exposure is 3 × 10¹⁴ incident particles. The nominal single-particle rate is 1 MHz. Actual running time depends on SHINE (Shanghai High Repetition-Rate XFEL (X-ray Free-Electron Laser) and Extreme Light Facility) operational inputs. A positron beamline is a proposed extension, and this study evaluates what it could add to the physics reach.

title: DarkSHINE detector concept
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# DarkSHINE detector concept
Measure the incident and recoil momenta, then veto visible energy in the calorimeters.
notes:
Following the beam through the detector, the tagging tracker measures the incoming momentum in the magnetic field. The particle then crosses a thin tungsten target, and the recoil tracker measures the outgoing charged particle. The ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) measures the remaining electromagnetic energy. The larger HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) provides enough material to detect penetrating hadrons and muons and reject those events. The trackers use strips, while the electromagnetic calorimeter uses a segmented crystal array. We use the simulation geometry to study their acceptance and response.

Click sequence: Tracking, ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter), HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter).

title: Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Detector requirements for a missing-energy search
SubsystemRequirement / benchmark
Tagging trackerHit resolution ; momentum resolution at 8 GeV
Tungsten target; limit multiple scattering
Recoil trackerAccept recoils from to 2 GeV; hit resolution
LYSO ECALContain e/γ showers; stochastic term after digitisation
Fe/scintillator HCALNeutron veto inefficiency for ; at lower energies
Acceptance gaps and calorimeter leakage can turn visible interactions into apparent missing energy.
Tracker momentum resolution and the ECAL stochastic term are simulation benchmarks; HCAL inefficiencies are neutron-veto design targets.
notes: These requirements come from the ways an ordinary interaction can look like missing energy. The tagging tracker needs a hit precision below 10 micrometres. Its reference simulation gives a momentum resolution below 2% at 8 GeV. The tungsten target is 0.1 radiation lengths thick to limit multiple scattering. The recoil tracker needs to measure soft tracks down to about 30 MeV, with acceptance extending to 2 GeV. The ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) contains electron and photon showers. Its digitised simulation gives a stochastic term below 2%; leakage into the low-energy tail needs a separate study. For the HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter), the neutron-veto inefficiency target is below 10⁻⁵ above roughly 2 GeV and below 10⁻³ at lower energies. The event background also depends on the neutron spectrum and the other selection cuts.

title: Electron-mode signal and background rejection
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Electron-mode signal and background rejection
SignalElectron beam

One soft recoil electron with substantial missing energy and momentum.

SelectionVisible vetoes

Measurements used together

  • Exactly one incident particle
  • A recoil carrying less momentum
  • Low electromagnetic energy
  • No significant hadronic or muon activity

Hard bremsstrahlung is abundant. Rare photonuclear, electronuclear and muon-pair processes can leave poorly measured energy.

The sensitivity is controlled by the rare surviving tails of Standard Model interactions.
J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023).
notes:
In electron mode, dark bremsstrahlung produces a dark photon that decays invisibly, together with a recoil electron. The recoil electron usually carries only part of the beam energy. Ordinary bremsstrahlung can also leave a soft electron, but the photon normally deposits its energy in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). The cases of concern are rare processes that transfer this energy to hadrons or muons, or send it outside the detector acceptance. We use the measured momentum, electromagnetic energy and HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) veto together to reject these events. The simulation needs to describe both the usual electromagnetic response and the rare shower tails that pass the cuts.

Presenter cue: Start with the signal diagram. Click once to introduce the combined detector requirements and backgrounds.
source: J. Chen et al., Sci. China Phys. Mech. Astron. 66, 211062 (2023).

title: Standard Model background hierarchy
body:
Physics motivation and DarkSHINE
# Standard Model background hierarchy

Two origins

Electronuclear interactions.

Hard bremsstrahlung followed by conversion or nuclear interactions.

Location matters

Target and ECAL processes encounter different veto material.
notes: Electronuclear interactions are one source of background. Another starts with hard bremsstrahlung, followed by pair conversion, a photonuclear interaction or muon-pair production. I show target and ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) interactions separately because the available veto material and the rates differ. The vertical scale gives approximate relative rates from the electron-mode study. The positron samples have their own normalisation. The small invisible electroweak contribution is shown separately from backgrounds caused by visible particles escaping detection. For the latter, we need enough simulated events in the rare branches and a way to recover their physical rates.

title: Event Simulation and Reconstruction in DarkSHINE
body:
02 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Event Simulation and
Reconstruction in DarkSHINE

A configurable chain for detector studies and rare-process production
notes: I will now describe our work on the simulation framework, from defining the detector and recording events to reducing the time needed to simulate rare backgrounds.

title: The DarkSHINE software framework
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# The DarkSHINE software framework
My contributions: DSimu, DEvent, rare-process biasing and filtering, and ACTS integration.
DSS software framework; X. Zhu, Nucl. Part. Phys. Proc. 346 (2024) 57.
notes: DSimu configures the detector and physics, runs the simulation, and writes events to ROOT files. DAna reads these files and runs digitisation, reconstruction and analysis in the chosen order. DEvent defines the collections shared between them, and DDis lets us inspect individual events. Our software work covers DSimu, the event model, rare-process biasing, staged filtering and ACTS (A Common Tracking Software) integration, as well as DAna, digitisation, the other tracking algorithms, calorimeter reconstruction and generator validation. With this common event interface, we can inspect an event at each stage. We can also rerun downstream algorithms without repeating transport, provided the files contain the information those algorithms need.
source: DSS software framework; X. Zhu, Nucl. Part. Phys. Proc. 346 (2024) 57.

title: A common event model: DEvent
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# A common event model: DEvent
Collection types distinguish Monte Carlo truth, detector deposits, response and reconstructed objects.
notes: DEvent is a container of physics object collections. McParticle and DStep store truth information, and SimulatedHit stores energy deposits from transport. CalorimeterHit contains the detector response, while ReconstructedParticle holds reconstructed objects. AnaEvent is currently an alias of DEvent. We use truth information to understand how a background event was produced, and measured or reconstructed quantities to select events. Collection names identify detector regions and response variants. Changing the input collection can therefore change what a reconstructed energy means, even with the same algorithm. We record the event schema and output choices with each production configuration.

title: Geometry and event-record optimisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Geometry and event-record optimisation
CPUGeometry navigation

Bounding volume hierarchy

Group detector volumes into nested bounding volumes to reduce navigation work.

260 → 42ms per event, without / with BVH
6.2×

Measured speed-up in the cited benchmark.

StoragePersistent event data

Record and memory layout

Optimise the stored data structure and memory alignment.

60.1 → 13.7KB per event, reported minimum
4.4×

Reduction for the cited event-record example.

Geometry navigation and event-record optimisation reduce CPU and storage costs.
notes: We have 2 main optimisations compared with the original baseline 1 DarkSHINE software. The first is a BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy). It groups detector volumes so Geant4 can rule out a large region before testing individual cells. In this benchmark, the simulation time falls from 260 to 42 milliseconds per event, about a factor of 6.2. The second improves the event record and memory alignment. The reported file size falls from 60.1 to as little as 13.7 kilobytes per event for that configuration. These benchmarks and the optical study shown later use different configurations, so we cannot multiply their speed-up factors together or treat them as results from a single release.

title: Generator-level filtering with staged transport
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Generator-level filtering with staged transport
Reject an event as soon as its production requirements fail, before transporting the full shower.
notes: The generator-level filter runs during particle transportation, before we write the full event to disk. At stage 0, we process only the primary track and keep its secondaries waiting. We can then check the primary interaction or energy loss. At stage 1, we process the relevant secondaries in the chosen region and check for the rare interaction we want. If the event passes, we transport the rest of the shower. We can also stop once the accumulated ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) energy exceeds an upper bound, because further deposits will only increase it. This saves time on events that we already know will fail the selection.

title: Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Rare-process biasing and physical normalisation
01Sampling

Sample the rare interaction

  • Select the process and detector region
  • Enhance its interaction probability
  • Retain the relevant secondary ancestry
  • Apply production filters within a defined domain
02Normalisation

Recover the physical prediction

The positron campaign uses dedicated process-rate normalisations, rather than the stored transport-weight field.

Biasing increases sampling frequency. Filtering defines which phase space is retained.
notes:
Biasing makes a chosen rare interaction happen more often in a specified region. We then correct the normalisation to recover the physical rate. For weighted event counting, the sum of weights gives the yield, and the sum of squared weights gives the Monte Carlo variance. A sample with many stored events can still have a much smaller effective event count. In the positron production, we use dedicated biasing studies and process cross sections for normalisation; we do not use the stored transport-weight field. Filtering also removes part of phase space. No weight can recover events we never generated, so the production cuts need to cover the phase space used in the analysis.

Presenter cue: Explain the biased sample first. Click once to show how the physical prediction is recovered.

notes: This production example uses 4 GeV electrons and processes 10¹¹ incident particles on 12,800 cores. Filtering reduces the estimated elapsed time from about 4 days to 15 hours. Storage falls from roughly 3 petabytes to 2.5 terabytes, and the disk write rate also decreases. These are approximate figures for different resource costs. The general filters reject events with too much visible energy or too little missing momentum. Dedicated filters also check for a particular particle or interaction. We save the filter acceptance and retained phase-space range with the sample, since we need them to interpret the output.

title: Parallel event simulation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Parallel event simulation
Production benchmark

10⁶ simulated events

8 threads, 1 job
15,328 s | 785% CPU

1 thread, 8 jobs
16,648 s | 646% CPU

~8%

Lower elapsed time with the same eight concurrent execution units.
notes: Geant4 can process several events in parallel within a single job. This required changes to thread-local allocation, singleton state, random-number handling and primary generation. In this benchmark, 1 job with 8 threads takes 15,328 seconds. Running 8 single-thread jobs takes 16,648 seconds. Both use 8 concurrent execution units, so the multi-thread job reduces elapsed time by about 8%. This is a comparison of job arrangements, rather than a scaling test from 1 core. We also compare inclusive and rare-process distributions to check that changing the worker count and scheduling preserves the physics.

title: Optical response with a lookup table
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Optical response with a lookup table

Precompute photon transport

Sample detection efficiency and transit time as functions of emission position and direction.

Response pathTime/event
Full optical tracking~200 s
LUT optical response~4 s
No optical photons~2 s

Detection efficiencies agree within 5% for the tested optical configuration.

About 50× faster than full optical tracking for the cited complete-event benchmark.
Credit: Qibin Liu
notes: Tracking every optical photon takes time because a single interaction can produce many photons. The lookup table avoids repeating that transport. It stores the detection probability and transit-time distribution for the simulated optical response. In this study, an event takes about 200 seconds with full optical tracking, 4 seconds with the table and 2 seconds without optical photons. The detection efficiencies shown on the left agree within 5%. This tests the table for the geometry and optical properties used to build it. Electronics effects and changes to the geometry need their own checks. The optical-response and digitisation studies are collaboration contributions integrated into the framework.

title: Digitisation connects deposits to observables
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Digitisation connects deposits to observables
From energy deposits

Response effects

Scintillation, collection efficiency, SiPM saturation and recovery, electronic noise, finite dynamic range and ADC sampling.

The production configuration selects the detailed optical or parameterised response.

The selected response collection and calibration define the meaning of reconstructed cell energy.
Credit: Qibin Liu
notes: Digitisation converts simulated energy deposits into detector signals. Light production and collection determine how many photons reach the sensor. The SiPM (Silicon Photomultiplier) response accounts for finite pixel occupancy and recovery. The electronics model then adds the waveform, noise, finite range and digitisation. We also have a parameterised response for samples that do not need full optical information. The production configuration records which model is used. In the positron analysis, we cut on both total energy and the largest cell deposit, so the response of individual cells near those thresholds matters.

title: Track finding and fitting
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Track finding and fitting
01Associate hits

Finding

Associate hits across tracker layers.
The legacy greedy finder ranks circle candidates and removes accepted hits.

02Estimate track parameters

Fitting

Estimate momentum and covariance with magnetic-field propagation, energy loss and multiple scattering.

GenFit Kalman fitting and a Riemann alternative are available.

Momentum residuals must compare reconstructed and reference states at the same surface.
Credit: Yifan Zhu
notes: Track finding decides which hits belong to the same track. The legacy algorithm for low-multiplicity events uses a quick circle pre-fit to rank candidates. Once it accepts a track, it removes those hits before looking for another. A full fit then calculates the track parameters using the magnetic field, material and measurement errors. The framework supports Kalman fitting with GenFit and an analytical Riemann fit. When checking momentum resolution, we compare the fitted and reference states at the same surface. We also use this convention when comparing tagging and recoil momenta across the target.

title: ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# ACTS integration in DarkSHINE
The independent sequencer uses truth-smeared seeds in its reference configuration.
My contributions: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.
notes: We integrated ACTS (A Common Tracking Software) through an independent sequencer and optional adapters in the existing Tracking processor. The sequencer converts the detector geometry into tracking surfaces and strip-pair hits into measurements and source links. The geometry, momenta and magnetic field all use the same coordinate mapping. The reference chain starts with truth-smeared seeds, runs combinatorial Kalman track finding, converts the trajectories and finds vertices. We can extrapolate recoil tracks to seed ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) clusters. Since the seeds use truth information, this chain does not give the efficiency of seeding from hits alone. The alternative space-point route still needs work and validation. These later tracking developments were not included in the frozen positron-analysis production.
source: Candidate contribution: ACTS sequencer, geometry/field adapters and reconstruction interfaces.

title: Signal generation and validation
body:
Event simulation and reconstruction
# Signal generation and validation
Validate both the production rate and kinematic distributions before applying detector selections.
Credit: Xiang Chen
notes: In the generator study by Xiang Chen, we compared the production cross section across mediator masses and the recoil-electron energy distributions. The cross section sets the expected rate, while the kinematics affect detector acceptance. When predicting selected events, we use a consistent production and detector-response configuration.

title: Positron-Beam-Mode Analysis
body:
03 / DISSERTATION PRE-DEFENCE

Positron-Beam-Mode
Analysis

Three production mechanisms, three exclusive reconstructed categories
notes: I will now use this simulation chain to study positron running. I will start with the additional production mechanisms and then follow them through the detector selection. We keep the baseline 1 detector so that we can compare with the published electron-beam projection using the same detector design.

title: Why a positron beam?
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Why a positron beam?
for an 8 GeV beam and an electron initially at rest.
X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900
notes:
A positron can undergo nuclear bremsstrahlung, just like an electron, and it can also annihilate with an atomic electron. Non-resonant annihilation produces a photon and a dark photon. In resonant annihilation, the electron and positron produce a dark photon that decays to a dark-matter pair, with no accompanying hard visible particle. For an electron initially at rest, an 8 GeV positron gives a centre-of-mass energy of about 90 MeV. This provides a mass scale that we do not have in the electron bremsstrahlung channel. To find the sensitivity gain, we also need to account for the visible final state, detector efficiency, migration between selections and positron backgrounds. I will compare the production rates and detector-level selections for these 3 mechanisms.

Presenter cue: Click 0: introduce dark bremsstrahlung, retained from electron running. Click 1: introduce non-resonant and resonant annihilation together, then explain the 90.4 MeV scale.

title: Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Production mechanisms at 8 GeV
Annihilation kinematics

Annihilation adds a mass scale

For an electron at rest,

Bound-electron motion broadens the annihilation kinematics.

The projection uses on-shell signal samples.

The radiative endpoint and resonant enhancement motivate a detector-level comparison near 90 MeV.
X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900.
notes: Nuclear bremsstrahlung covers a broad range of mediator masses. Non-resonant annihilation is limited by the available centre-of-mass energy, and resonant production is enhanced near that energy. An 8 GeV positron annihilating with an electron at rest has a centre-of-mass energy of 90.4 MeV. Bound electrons are moving, which broadens this picture and allows the resonant samples to extend above the stationary-electron value. We generate on-shell mediators in this study. We do not include a separate off-shell dark-matter-pair calculation. We then apply the detector selection to find the accepted yield for each mechanism.
source: X. Zhu et al., arXiv:2609.05900. Original cross-section plot.

title: Signal and background samples
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal and background samples
Efficiency samples

Signal grid

MechanismMass points
Dark bremsstrahlung30
Non-resonant annihilation18
Resonant annihilation23

events per channel–mass point.

CalcHEP kinematics followed by Geant4 transport.

Background predictions

Background production

  • PN, EN and muon-pair conversion
  • Target/tracker and ECAL locations
  • Additional target-annihilation sample
  • Independent inclusive sample: POT

Common benchmark: 8 GeV, POT, baseline 1 detector.

Equal generated signal counts measure efficiency. Cross sections determine the physical mixture.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes: We simulate 30 bremsstrahlung mass points, 18 non-resonant points and 23 resonant points, with 100,000 events at each point. We calculate efficiencies from these equal-sized samples and apply the physical rates afterwards. For backgrounds, we generate dedicated biased samples of photonuclear, positron-nuclear and muon-pair processes. Production in the target or tracker is separate from production in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). The EN (Electronuclear) label is retained for the positron-nuclear sample in this campaign. We also generate ordinary annihilation in the target. An independent inclusive sample contains the equivalent of 2.5 × 10⁹ incident positrons. We use it to check the dedicated predictions without adding it to the background total. All sensitivity results use baseline 1.

title: Three exclusive signal regions
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Three exclusive signal regions
SelectionSR1: recoil positronSR2: photon-likeSR3: low activity
Tagging tracks= 1= 1= 1
Recoil tracks= 1= 0= 0
Missing momentum> 4 GeV——
ECAL total energy< 2.5 GeV< 2 GeV< 2 GeV
ECAL maximum cell—≥ 1 MeV< 1 MeV
HCAL total energy< 100 MeV< 100 MeV< 100 MeV
HCAL maximum cell< 1 MeV< 1 MeV< 1 MeV
Track multiplicity separates SR1. Complementary ECAL maximum-cell cuts separate SR2 and SR3.
notes: We assign events to reconstructed categories without using the generated process label. Every category requires exactly 1 tagging track. SR1 (Signal Region 1) requires 1 recoil track and missing momentum above 4 GeV. SR2 (Signal Region 2) and SR3 (Signal Region 3) require 0 recoil tracks and total ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) energy below 2 GeV. We divide these samples at a maximum-cell energy of 1 MeV, with events on the boundary assigned to region 2. Every region also requires low total HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) energy and no cell above 1 MeV. The selections do not overlap. Events with additional tracks or a failed veto are rejected.

title: Momentum and total-energy discrimination
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Momentum and total-energy discrimination
The production filter requires missing momentum > 1 GeV. The final SR1 requirement is > 4 GeV.
arXiv:2609.05900
notes: On the left is missing momentum. The background sample already passes the loose production filter at 1 GeV; the final analysis cut is 4 GeV. On the right is the total ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) energy for non-resonant annihilation. Near the mediator-mass endpoint, the accompanying photon is soft. The 90 MeV signal can therefore pass a low-energy cut even though a photon is produced. The detector response and acceptance determine the fraction that passes.

title: Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Maximum-cell energy separates the zero-track sample
defines SR2; defines SR3.
notes: For events with no recoil track, the largest ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) cell helps distinguish a photon deposit from a nearly empty calorimeter. The non-resonant distribution changes with mediator mass because the photon kinematics change. Resonant annihilation usually leaves little activity, although interactions in the tracker material can produce deposits. We also cut on total energy because many small deposits can add up. The 1 MeV cuts assume that the detector can operate at those thresholds; they are not measured noise levels. The campaign does not fully digitise HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) noise and pileup, so detector measurements are needed to test this assumption.

title: Signal efficiency across the mass scan
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal efficiency across the mass scan
All nine channel-to-region efficiencies enter the signal prediction.
notes: These curves show the cutflow efficiency for each production mechanism in its primary region. Each curve is normalised to the generated sample. We apply the cross sections later to obtain the expected mixture of processes. The backups contain all 9 channel-to-region efficiency curves. An event can enter a different region if its recoil track is not reconstructed, or if its photon escapes detection or falls below threshold. For example, bremsstrahlung can enter the regions with no recoil track. Its efficiency in the low-activity region becomes substantial toward the upper end of the mass grid. We include these migrations when predicting the signal. The next slide gives the expected yields at 90 MeV.

title: Signal migration at 90 MeV
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Signal migration at 90 MeV
||
At 90 MeV, non-resonant annihilation supplies about 95% of SR2; resonant annihilation supplies about 84% of SR3.
notes: At 90 MeV, non-resonant annihilation supplies about 95% of SR2 (Signal Region 2), and resonant annihilation supplies about 84% of SR3 (Signal Region 3). Bremsstrahlung contributes very little at this mass. The matrix includes events that migrate away from the primary region of their production mechanism. The entries are expected event counts at a fixed reference coupling, after applying the rates and efficiencies. They are not raw simulation counts.

title: Background rejection in the available simulation
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Background rejection in the available simulation
PN ECAL | cumulative unweighted simulated counts
No simulated events survive the full selection; the residual background is estimated by extrapolation.
notes: This cutflow follows photonuclear interactions in the ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter). The recoil-track cut first divides events into categories with 1 or 0 recoil tracks. The next cut uses momentum in SR1 (Signal Region 1), the maximum-cell lower bound in SR2 (Signal Region 2) and total electromagnetic energy in SR3 (Signal Region 3). The HCAL (Hadronic Calorimeter) veto reduces the samples further, and the final electromagnetic-energy cut removes the remaining simulated events. These bars are unweighted simulation counts, before scaling to the benchmark exposure. No event in the inclusive or dedicated samples passes a complete region selection. Because the samples are finite, this does not imply that the physical background is 0.

title: Normalisation checked in populated sidebands
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Normalisation checked in populated sidebands
Rate validation

Independent comparison

Dedicated samples are normalised using process rates and filter acceptance.

The inclusive sample tests the populated survival trend.

The two routes describe the same backgrounds and are not added together.

Sideband agreement supports the production model where simulated events remain.
notes: We normalise each dedicated sample to its equivalent unbiased exposure using the number of generation attempts, generator acceptance and physical branching ratio. The number of attempts differs from the number of stored events, so we keep track of both. We then compare the sum of the dedicated samples, including target annihilation, with the independent inclusive sample where enough events are available. This checks the rates and shapes in that region. It does not test the much smaller tails at the final cuts. We use the inclusive sample for this cross-check only, since adding it to the dedicated samples would count the same background twice.

notes: For SR1 (Signal Region 1) and SR2 (Signal Region 2), we fit the dedicated survival curves with a power law in the total-ECAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter) threshold, expressed in MeV. The nominal predictions are 0.03 events for region 1 and 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ for region 2. SR3 (Signal Region 3) needs a 2-dimensional fit because total energy and maximum-cell energy are correlated. Its nominal prediction is 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ events. These estimates depend on the chosen fit function and the limited tail statistics. They also omit components with no surviving simulated events. The inclusive 1-dimensional comparison uses an exponential fit, so it does not provide a quantitative closure test at the final thresholds.

notes:
At each mass, we sum the contributions from all 3 production mechanisms in every region. A common signal-strength parameter scales them because their rates depend on the same kinetic mixing. We use a binned profile likelihood with nuisance parameters to obtain expected 90% CL (Confidence Level) limits using CLs (the modified frequentist confidence-level method) under the background-only hypothesis. The reported construction treats shape uncertainties as uncorrelated between bins and uses a Poisson prescription for background normalisation. The regions do not share events, although detector uncertainties can be correlated between them.

title: Scope of the positron projection
body:
Positron-beam-mode analysis
# Scope of the positron projection
Simulation result

Established within this study

  • Full detector-level signal efficiencies
  • Three exclusive categories with migration
  • Dedicated and inclusive sideband comparison
  • A combined 8 GeV benchmark projection
Experimental inputs

Inputs requiring further validation

  • Background extrapolation into empty tails
  • Rare components omitted after zero survivors
  • 1 MeV HCAL cell threshold with noise and pileup
  • Low-count coverage of the asymptotic likelihood
notes: This study gives detector-level efficiencies and migration between regions for the 3 production mechanisms in the benchmark setup. We use them to obtain the combined sensitivity. The largest remaining uncertainties are the small background tails and the assumed veto response. Larger rare-process samples would help constrain the extrapolation and the omitted components. Prototype measurements can test the thresholds with realistic noise and pileup. We also need toy Monte Carlo to check the statistical treatment at very low event counts. These studies will help assess how closely an experimental search can reach the projection.

title: Main results
body:
Summary and outlook
# Main results
Software result

A common event-processing chain

Configurable transport and DEvent interfaces connect detector studies to reconstruction and analysis.

Geometry optimisation, staged filters, biasing and parallel execution make rare-process production practical.

ACTS interfaces support tracking and calorimeter matching.

Physics result

Additional annihilation channels

Three exclusive signal regions retain all production-to-category migrations.

Expected 90% CL reach at 90 MeV and POT.
notes: We developed a configurable simulation framework and event model that connect transport to detector response and reconstruction. Geometry and event-record optimisation reduce the cost per event. Biasing and staged filters make rare-background production more practical, and parallel processing increases the production capacity. We also integrated ACTS (A Common Tracking Software) into the reconstruction framework. Using this simulation chain, we studied positron running with 3 exclusive regions and included migration between them. At 90 MeV, the combined expected limit is 5.33 × 10⁻¹³ in epsilon squared at the benchmark exposure. Annihilation gives most of the improvement, especially the non-resonant contribution near its endpoint, under the assumptions discussed earlier.

title: Outlook
body:
Summary and outlook
# Outlook
Detector response

Constrain digitisation, calibration and veto thresholds with prototype and beam-test data.

Rare backgrounds

Extend dedicated samples and quantify the stability of sideband extrapolations.

Statistical model

Validate the low-count limit with toy Monte Carlo and explicit modelling uncertainties.

Beam-energy scan

Re-evaluate signal, acceptance and backgrounds at additional positron energies.

The annihilation mass scale varies as the square root of the beam energy.
notes: Detector measurements will help constrain the response and veto thresholds. Larger rare-process samples will improve our estimate of the background tails and their dependence on the fit model. Toy Monte Carlo can test the statistical approximation when expected backgrounds are small. Another option is to vary the beam energy. The characteristic annihilation mass changes approximately with the square root of the beam energy, so an energy scan could probe other masses. Each energy would need a study of its kinematics, acceptance and backgrounds. The 8 GeV analysis and the simulation framework provide a starting point.
